title: Shemot: the lost lamb (Exodus Rabbah 2:2)
hookLine: midrash: Moses carries a runaway lamb back, and God chooses him to shepherd a people

lines: HOW DO YOU PICK A LEADER?
cards: How do you pick a leader? A job interview. A résumé.
A vote, a speech, a debate. The big moments.
The Torah tells us Moses grew up in Pharaoh's palace, killed an Egyptian who was beating a Hebrew slave, fled to the desert, married, and became a shepherd for his father-in-law, Jethro.
Then one day God speaks to him from a burning bush and sends him to free a nation. The Torah doesn't say why him. The rabbis wanted to know.

teach.b: The story is a midrash, a rabbinic teaching that fills a gap in the text, from a collection called Exodus Rabbah. Moses is tending Jethro's flock in the wilderness. One little animal slips away and runs.
The midrash actually says a young goat; it's often retold as a lamb. Moses goes after it. It runs and runs, until it reaches a shady spot with a pool of water, and stops to drink.
And Moses, out of breath, says: I didn't know you were running because you were thirsty. You must be exhausted.
He picks it up, puts it on his shoulders, and carries it all the way back to the flock. That's the whole story. No miracle, no speech.
And the midrash says God saw it and said: you have compassion to lead a flock that belongs to a man.
By your life, you will shepherd my flock, Israel. Notice what Moses didn't do. He didn't scold the runaway.
He didn't leave it, though it was one animal out of many.

He assumed the running had a reason, and the reason was need. The same midrash tells a similar story about David, the shepherd boy who became king: he let the youngest sheep eat the tender grass first.
In this telling, you don't find a leader on a stage. You find one when nobody is watching, when somebody small wanders off, and someone goes after them.

how: Jewish tradition calls Moses Moshe Rabbeinu, Moses our teacher, and often calls him the faithful shepherd; midrashim like this one are taught to children and adults alike to explain what the Torah leaves unsaid.

games.q: you're Moses, alone with a big flock. one small animal bolts into the desert. what do you do?
o: let it go; there are plenty more.
chase it, and carry it back.
games.why: in the midrash, Moses chased it to a pool, realized it was thirsty, and carried it home on his shoulders. God chose him to shepherd Israel.

practice: Bring to mind someone who has drifted from a group you're part of: the friend who stopped coming, the relative who went quiet, the classmate who's always a few steps behind.
Instead of wondering what's wrong with them, ask Moses's question: what are they thirsty for? Then choose one small way to go after them.

wordCard.voice: Shemot. The portion where Moses, a shepherd in the desert, is chosen to lead; a midrash says it was because he carried back a runaway lamb.

orig.note: Hebrew: shepherd. What Moses was when God called him, and what the midrash says he became for a people.
